extracted.intended_audience: newsroom editors, journalists, social media managers, platform users and product/ML teams interested in how X identifies trending topics
extracted.subtask_description: Understand the signals and implicit newsworthiness criteria X (Twitter) uses to surface trending topics so newsrooms and product teams can interpret, monitor, and act on trends responsibly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume + Velocity (Key)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sharp spikes in activity (velocity) are prioritized over slow, high absolute volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A topic that generates a sudden burst (e.g., 10,000 tweets in 1 hour) will trend faster than one that accumulates a larger number of tweets over days. Emphasize rapid change over cumulative totals when judging whether a topic will surface as a trend; velocity is the dominant signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement Quality and Intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Types of engagement carry different weight: retweets, quote tweets, and replies are weighted higher than simple mentions or likes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replies and conversational activity indicate stronger interest than passive interactions. High-intensity engagement (many replies/quotes) suggests active public discussion and is more newsworthy for trend detection than just volume of likes or mentions.

rubrics_metrics.name: User Diversity / Network Diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity of users participating in the conversation — not just a single or homogeneous cluster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trends that involve many distinct users, accounts from different communities, or influencers across networks are stronger signals than activity concentrated in one tightly connected group. Use diversity to detect organic spread vs. echo-chamber amplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-cluster Spread (Non‑single-cluster propagation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Topics that spread across multiple social clusters/networks are prioritized over those confined to a single cluster.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-cluster spread indicates broader public interest; lack of spread suggests a topic may be niche or artificially amplified. This helps distinguish organic virality from coordinated or siloed campaigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalization (Local and Individual Relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trending results are personalized based on who you follow, your inferred interests, and your location; trends are both local and personalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A trend may surface differently for different users — editors should interpret X trends as a mix of global, local, and personalized signals. When monitoring for breaking news, check local and broader views rather than relying on a single personalized feed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation Detection / Authenticity Signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Bot networks, coordinated inauthentic behavior, and artificial boosting are detected and penalized; fake trending is removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithmic filters downweight or exclude activity that appears automated or coordinated. Presence of bot-like accounts, sudden coordinated posting from related accounts, or other inauthentic signals reduces a topic's legitimacy as a news signal. This is an anti-manipulation criterion to protect trend quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recency / Real-time Prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: Trends represent what is popular now; older topics decay over time via a decay function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real-time relevance is prioritized. Even high-volume historical topics lose prominence as the algorithm applies decay to older activity. For editorial use, treat X trends primarily as immediate, time‑sensitive indicators rather than long-term importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic Concentration (Local vs Global Spread)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographic distribution matters: a trend may be locally concentrated or globally spread, and both are meaningful in different ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local concentration can identify region-specific breaking events (e.g., local disaster) while global spread signals broader cultural or international events. Editors should distinguish local trends from global ones when deciding coverage scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Events Indicative of Newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain event types commonly surface as trends: breaking events (shootings, disasters), sports moments, celebrity events, political controversies, cultural memes, and hashtag campaigns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these exemplars as heuristics for what the crowd treats as newsworthy in real time. They are not guarantees of journalistic importance — each item still needs verification and editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative Signals — What Trends Are Not Quality News
rubrics_metrics.description: Manipulated trends, outrage-bait, algorithm-gamed hashtags, and coordinated promotion are examples of trending activity that do not equal high-quality news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious: viral does not equal verified or important. Treat topics suspected of being driven by coordination, gaming, or outrage-bait as lower editorial priority until authenticated. This is an anti-pattern list for newsroom filtering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit Newsworthiness Criteria Summarized
rubrics_metrics.description: The algorithm implicitly uses signals such as velocity of conversation, cross-cluster spread, engagement intensity (replies > likes), geographic concentration or global spread, authenticity signals, real-time relevance, and user network diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These summarized criteria are a checklist for why a topic might be surfaced. Newsrooms can map these signals to verification and editorial value assessments—for instance, high velocity + broad network diversity + authenticity = stronger lead for coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grok AI — AI-generated 'Grok Analysis' Explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Grok AI provides AI summaries that explain why a topic is trending by pulling context from thousands of posts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Grok Analysis as a rapid context signal to understand drivers of a trend, but apply journalistic verification since AI summaries can omit nuance or propagate errors. Treat AI explanations as augmenting human investigation, not replacing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: How Newsrooms Should Use Trends (Editorial Implications & Risks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trending topics can drive editorial decisions (tip source for breaking events; audience-feedback signal), but present risks: 'tail wagging the dog' coverage, verification challenges, and information disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trends as a source for monitoring and tip collection, not as sole justification for coverage. Implement verification workflows, be aware of audience-driven incentives, and guard against giving disproportionate attention to manipulated or low-quality viral items.
